Bilk

/BILK/ - rhymes with silk · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Bilk means to cheat someone out of money.

The ticket broker bilked hundreds of fans, collecting full price for seats in rows the stadium did not contain.

Worked Example

The clinic's billing office bilked the insurance company for a decade, charging for therapy sessions on days when the building was locked.

Bilk is specifically about money slipping away through cheating. Overcharging is greedy but open, and to shortchange is to skim a little — to bilk is to take money for something that was never real: sessions never held, seats that never existed.

How Bilk Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

swindle

swindle: cheating by scheme, big or small — the everyday word

defraud

defraud: the formal, courtroom term for the same act

Antonyms

reimburse

reimburse: hands money back instead of taking it

repay

repay: settles a debt honestly and in full

How Strong Is It? — shortchange → bilk → fleece

shortchange vs. bilk

shortchange vs. bilk: Shortchange is milder than bilk — a shortchanged customer is out a few coins at the register, more insult than injury.

fleece vs. bilk

fleece vs. bilk: Fleece goes further than bilk: a bilked victim loses money, but a fleeced one is stripped bare, the way a sheep loses its whole coat in one shearing.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — bilk

Root — bilk: to spoil an opponent's score (17th-century cribbage slang, perhaps a twisting of balk)

Put it together

Put it together: Bilk has no parts to peel: it surfaced in the 1650s as a cribbage player's word for spoiling an opponent's score, perhaps a twisted pronunciation of balk, 'to block.' From the card table it moved to the marketplace — blocking people from money that is rightfully theirs. The word is its own root.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Because bilk began as gaming slang rather than as a Latin or Greek root, it never grew a family — no prefix, no suffix, no cousins. If another word looks like bilk, it is probably milk, and the two have nothing to do with each other.

Strength Check

Word Choice

informal / punchy

Bilk is a compact, headline-flavored verb for cheating people out of money — it wants a victim and a sum. Swindle works almost anywhere bilk does; defraud is what the indictment will say. And when the price was merely outrageous rather than stolen, overcharge is the honest word.
